title: From the adjacent sandssh sweep: two items that are dropssh's, and one that is already done
body:
# From the adjacent sandssh sweep: two items that are dropssh's, and one that is already done

Research unit, 2026-09-28 (method: TEMPLATE `docs/methodology/research.md`).
**Evidence. Nothing implemented.** The issue 1 sweep was run against
`talaria0101/sandssh`'s open issues as well, because two of them name
dropssh's backlog explicitly. Of the items they raise, **one is already done**,
**two are dropssh's to adopt**, and the rest is filed elsewhere.

## Provenance

| source | what it is | how it was checked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sandssh #12 (2026-09-28) | "This tree: same one-session gap … carry the proxy-aware ws + env-token forward" | read, then **checked against dropssh's source at `1329927ff41c`** |
| sandssh #6 (2026-09-28) | wiretap, and "adopt the operator-side SOCKS capability" | read; the SOCKS half is re-derived and scoped in dropssh #4 |
| dropssh itself | the subject | built (`exit 0`) and gated (`tests/e2e.sh`, 9 passed, 0 failed) on this machine, 2026-09-28 |

## ⛔ Already done: the env-var relay token. Do not re-open it.

sandssh #12 asks that dropssh carry an **env-var token** forward
(`SANDSSH_RELAY_KEY`) so a token does not have to appear on a command line.

**dropssh already reads one, and reads it before the parser runs** —
`src/main.c:133-136`:

```c
o.token = getenv("DROPSSH_TOKEN");
if (o.token == NULL) {
    o.token = getenv("DROPSSH_RELAY_TOKEN");
}
```

and `--token` overrides it (`main.c:155-157`), and the token is sent as
`X-Relay-Token` "never in a URL" (`main.c:45`). ⛔ **Nothing to do.** Recorded
because a later session reading sandssh #12 would otherwise file it as new work
against a tree that already has it. The one adjacent-repo suggestion that is
*not* carried across is sandssh's `--insecure` flag, and dropssh correctly has
one (`--insecure`, off by default, `main.c:49`) — sandssh #12 itself says to
carry the env var and **not** the flag.

## ⭐ Item 1 — the operator-side SOCKS, scoped for dropssh (adopt, from #4)

Already argued and scoped in the wiretap issue (**#4**). Repeated here only to
place it in the backlog, because it is the one **new capability** this whole
sweep produced that dropssh does not have.

* **Where it goes:** the **operator** side. `dropssh relay` binds the listener,
  so it must be a relay verb option, not a cage-side one — a cage cannot bind
  INET at all (dropssh #6, measured).
* **What it costs:** a SOCKS5 `CONNECT` parse (the request is a fixed
  4+ bytes plus a domain or 4-byte address) and a `reject` on anything the
  relay is not allowed to reach. There is no new transport and no new
  dependency.
* **The decision to make on purpose:** whether forwards survive a relay
  restart. wiretap's `README.md:481` is explicit that they do not ("If a
  Wiretap Server process exits or dies for any reason it will not remember
  ports it was previously exposing"). dropssh's relay holds no such state
  today, so **doing nothing is a valid answer** and the honest one for a
  single-tenant relay; adopting the SOCKS does not force the choice.
* ⛔ **Not a cage capability.** The listener can never be in the cage, so
  "reverse SOCKS" is not a thing dropssh can ship. This is the correction to
  the framing in sandssh #6.

## ⚠ Item 2 — the same-session gap is shared, and dropssh is the more capable tree (confirms)

sandssh #12's substantive claim: both trees have the **same one-session gap**
(serves a socketpair, tears down, redials — dropssh **B1**), and
**"dropssh is the more capable of the two"**.

⛔ **Verified against dropssh's source, not taken on the wording.** B1 is
`docs/relay-issues.md:30-40` and the code is `src/serve.c:264-353`
(`do_session` returns after one session; the `for(;;)` loop at `:384` redials).
**Confirmed.** The second claim — that dropssh is the more capable tree — is
**evidence of intent, not something this session measured**: it is a
comparison between two trees this unit did not build side by side. It is
**plausible** (dropssh has three patches, a real gate, and a multiplexer
design note; the python tree has a working `--transport ws`), and what would
settle it is a session on both trees against the same relay, which was **not
done here**.

## ⛔ Filed elsewhere, not here

* ⛔ **The multiplexed reverse path (B1–B5)** stays in `docs/relay-issues.md`.
  sandssh #3 and #12 both say implement it once, in dropssh, in C. Nothing in
  the issue 1 corpus displaces that.
* ⛔ **The relay's close-code correction (1009, `bad multiplex frame`)** is
  sandssh #3's finding against dropssh's docs. It is a **documentation**
  correction in five places, not new work from this sweep, and it is
  **not re-derived here**: this unit did not run the relay, so it neither
  confirms nor disputes the measurement. A session that wants to act on it
  should read sandssh #3 and reproduce `poc/10-reverse-relay-multiplex.js`
  first.

## ⛔ What was NOT established

* **sandssh was not built or run.** Its issues were read; its tree was not
  fetched this session. Every claim about *dropssh* above is checked against
  dropssh's source; every claim about *sandssh* is sandssh's own wording and is
  marked as such.
* **The SOCKS was not implemented or tested.** The scope above is an estimate
  for the implementing session, not a proof it works.
* **"dropssh is the more capable tree" is not measured** (see above).
* The 1009 close-code claim is **passed through, not verified** — deliberately,
  because verifying it needs the live relay and this unit is a triage.

title: Verdict on issue 1: three of the four are refused, one mechanism is adopted, and the plan does not change
body:
# Verdict on issue 1: three of the four are refused, one mechanism is adopted, and the plan does not change

Research unit, 2026-09-28. Method: TEMPLATE `docs/methodology/research.md`.
**Evidence. Nothing implemented.** This is the umbrella issue: it answers
issue 1 and points at the four per-reference issues, which carry the
provenance, the findings, the adopt/refuse lists and the "not established"
lists.

## The question, and the answer in one line

> Which mechanism from `dropbear-sshj`, `wiretap#tcp-tunneling`, `websocat` /
> the Cloudflare recipe, or `dropbear-hacks` can be moved into dropssh's C, at
> what cost, and **what breaks it in a cage with no INET bind, no `/dev/ptmx`,
> no `/etc/passwd`, no resolver, and 443-only egress?**

**One mechanism is adoptable, and it is worth more than all three refusals put
together: dropbear-hacks' `FAKE_ROOT`, validated end to end on the pinned
dropbear.** The other three are refused, each with a measured reason rather
than a preference.

| reference | verdict | issue | the deciding reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **dropbear-hacks** | **adopt the mechanism, refuse the code** | #2 | It **changes the observable login outcome** on the pinned dropbear 2026.94, through a real ssh session, with `LD_PRELOAD` unset. R9's premise is now evidence. |
| dropbear-sshj | refused | #3 | One commit, one author, self-described "bad, use sish" — and it sets `allowprivport = 1`, which changes the security posture of the very function R9 patches. |
| wiretap | architecture refused, one capability adoptable | #4 | WireGuard TUN + UDP is refused on measured 443-only egress; the server-side SOCKS is a **dropssh** feature on the operator, not a wiretap import. |
| websocat + Cloudflare | refused | #5 | It is a bridge, not a tunneler. It **confirms B4** from a second language and **confirms B7** (its own `README.md:535` and issues #35/#13). We already have a better first-party hop. |

## What this does NOT change

⛔ **`docs/relay-issues.md` is still the plan.** B1–B5 (the multiplexed
reverse path) remain the work, B4 remains the root cause, and R1–R11 are
unaffected. **No reference in issue 1 displaces that**, and none of them
argues for a second transport. The two earlier sweeps in this project reached
the same conclusion from the other side of the category; this one, from inside
it, reaches it again.

⛔ **Feature parity is not the goal and was not attempted.** Issue 1 asks to
"match feature parity/exceed ours" with four projects. Two of them (wiretap,
websocat) are **not ssh servers** and have no feature set to match: one is a
WireGuard mesh, one is a byte-stream bridge. The only two that touch dropbear
are a fork that declines to be used and a patch that is a superset of a
mechanism dropssh already ships out of process. **Taken together the corpus
says the parity question is malformed for three of the four references**, and
that is the useful answer.

## The one thing that is genuinely new

**R9 stops being a hunch.** `docs/open-issues.md` calls it "the best remaining
change to the product". It is now measured:

* the mechanism's 4 applicable hunks land on the pinned dropbear, and
  **all three of FAKE_ROOT's own files are among them**;
* it compiles;
* the stock server logs `Login attempt for nonexistent user` and the
  FAKE_ROOT server logs `Pubkey auth succeeded for 'root'` and returns uid 0,
  **both with the shim absent**, through dropssh's own `serve` and `connect`.

⛔ **And the safe version is not FAKE_ROOT.** It is a passwd **file** — which
dropssh's `--passwd FILE` already has the shape of, and which `fakepwd.so`
already implements out of process. FAKE_ROOT hard-codes uid 0 for anyone who
asks for `root`; fine for a one-user cage, wrong the moment the server answers
to more than one name. **The finding is "in-tree beats LD_PRELOAD", not
"ship FAKE_ROOT".** The proof of concept is a transcription, not a patch, and
it deliberately does not build the `--passwd-file` option R9 actually asks for.

## What was refused, and the shape of the refusals

All three refusals are structural, and all three name a **measured** wall rather
than a preference:

* **no INET `bind`** (a TCP listener in the cage) — measured today, and the
  reason websocat's "local listener" variant and a Cloudflare worker's cage
  side are dead;
* **no UDP egress, and 443 only** — measured twice with the proxy's own status
  line, which is why WireGuard is out;
* **a TUN device and privileged routing** — the reason gVisor netstack is
  pointless here: it exists to present a routed IP interface, and ssh gives a
  byte stream and a login.

⛔ **Correction to this project's own wording, made because it changes a
verdict:** the host is **not** "bindless". AF_UNIX `bind`+`listen` succeed at
uid 0 and carry real bytes. The precise constraint is *no INET bind*, and a
unix-socket relay works here. See the host-conditions issue (#6), which also
records three of my own instruments failing first and being replaced.

## ⛔ What was NOT established

* **One machine, one day**, and it is a stand-in for the target cage, not the
  cage itself.
* **No reference was run as a project.** The one exception is the FAKE_ROOT
  mechanism, which was transcribed, built and driven through a real session.
* **The Cloudflare any-TCP recipe was not read or tested.** It is a web page,
  not a repository. The verdict does not depend on it.
* **dropbear-sshj's tracker is unreachable.** Bitbucket's issues API is
  deprecated (verified: `CHANGE-3071`). A real gap in the sweep.
* **No interactive session anywhere**: no `/dev/ptmx` here, so every session is
  a command session, and `pty_setowner` on the FAKE_ROOT path is untested.
* **Nothing was tested against the real ajam relay.**
* **Two earlier verdicts in this project's trackers were wrong or overstated**
  (both in #6). That is the only honest estimate of how many of the claims
  above are still wrong: assume more remain.

## The three reviews, for the whole sweep

Each lens reports what it looked at that the others did not.

* **The door sweep.** For the one adopted mechanism, every `getpwnam`/
  `getpwuid` in the pinned dropbear was enumerated: **seven**, of which
  FAKE_ROOT patches **three**. The other four were then read rather than
  assumed harmless, and all four already degrade (null-checked `pw`, `HOME`
  from the environment, or a logged warning). So the patch author's three call
  sites are exactly the ones that hard-fail, and a patch covering all seven
  would be four lines longer and fix nothing. **What would have made this pass
  find more:** a `getpwnam` dereferenced without a null check. It searched all
  of `src/*.c`; none exists.
* **The guard mutation.** The PoC's "the mechanism was inserted" guard was
  **broken and is now fixed**. Planted defect: an insertion that cannot fire.
  First run: reported `CONFIRMED` with `0 call site(s) patched`, because a stale
  build directory made "the FAKE_ROOT dropbear" an old binary. Fixed (clean
  tree per run, hard `fallback call sites inserted >= 2`), then re-tested:
  the mutation now **exits 1**, the correct input **exits 0**. Both read
  unpiped.
* **The claim audit.** Every `file:line` in the four issues was re-resolved
  against the captured commits, and **two were wrong and are corrected**
  (`common-session.c:145`→`:148`, `svr-auth.c:95-99`→`:98-100`). The
  "5 failing files are all ALT_SHELL/master-password and none touch FAKE_ROOT"
  claim was verified per file, not by eye. One draft sentence claiming "0
  discussions" for dropbear-hacks was checked against the corpus before filing
  and confirmed (the `1` from `jq length` was the wrapper object's keys).

## Where the evidence is

Under `/tmp/dropssh-triage`, outside the repository and outside git, as
instructed. It is **not** committed and **not** pushed:

```
corpus/     the four trees at the captured commits + dropssh itself
experiments/10,20,30,40,50   the measurements, each with a question in its header
poc/10-dropbear-hacks-fake-root.sh   the one PoC; exit 0 = confirmed
findings/00-findings.md    the full write-up with all three reviews
```

⛔ **Say plainly: the corpus is on one machine's /tmp and is not in the
repository.** The method prefers a tracked corpus, and this task's instruction
was to use a tmp path and keep it out of git. The honest trade: every claim
above names its commit, its file and its line, and each measurement is a script
that re-runs and prints its own conditions — so a later session can re-derive
any of it without this directory. That is weaker than a tracked corpus and it
is the cost of the instruction, stated rather than hidden.

## The exact commands, on this machine

```sh
sh experiments/10-probe-the-cage.sh           # the conditions
sh experiments/20-bind-tcp-vs-unix.sh         # INET vs UNIX bind
sh experiments/30-confirm-no-raw-sockets.sh   # control: bytes over AF_UNIX
sh experiments/40-confirm-egress-allowlist.sh # 443-only, two rounds
sh experiments/50-login-outcome.sh unpatched  # the login, without the mechanism
sh poc/10-dropbear-hacks-fake-root.sh         # the PoC; exit 0 = confirmed
```

title: Measured: the cage constraints, and two corrections to what this project already believes about them
body:
# Measured: the cage constraints, and two corrections to what this project already believes about them

Research unit, 2026-09-28. Method: TEMPLATE `docs/methodology/research.md`.
**These are the conditions, not recommendations.** Filed separately because
every verdict in the issue 1 sweep rests on them, and because **two of them
contradict what this project's own trackers say.**

One machine, one day: **Linux 6.18.54, uid 0, 2026-09-28, zig 0.13.0**.
Re-run any of the five scripts below; each prints its own conditions.

## ⛔ Correction 1: "the cage cannot bind(2) even at uid 0" is TOO STRONG

**The measurement.** At uid 0:

```
AF_INET   0.0.0.0:0        FAIL  errno=13 (EACCES)  Permission denied
AF_INET   127.0.0.1:0      FAIL  errno=13 (EACCES)  Permission denied
AF_INET   127.0.0.1:51999  FAIL  errno=13 (EACCES)  Permission denied
AF_INET6  ::1:0            FAIL  errno=13 (EACCES)  Permission denied
AF_UNIX   /tmp/...         OK
AF_UNIX   abstract ('@')   OK
AF_UNIX   listen(4)        OK
socket(AF_INET) create     OK
socketpair                 OK
```

**`experiments/20-bind-tcp-vs-unix.sh`**, and a control in
`experiments/30-confirm-no-raw-sockets.sh` that carries **real bytes between
forked processes over an AF_UNIX socket**, and reads them back.

**Three candidate explanations, tested before any of them was adopted:**

| | explanation | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C1 | seccomp filters `bind(2)` for AF_INET only | **confirmed** — every INET family refused with EACCES at the same uid, same instant, as AF_UNIX succeeding |
| C2 | a privilege or userns problem, not a filter | **REFUTED** — it would fail AF_UNIX too, and it did not. Not uid. |
| C3 | a capability / port-range policy | **REFUTED** — a fixed high port (51999, which needs no capability) fails identically to an ephemeral one, so it is not a port-range rule |
| C4 | the process is killed (SECCOMP_RET_KILL) | **REFUTED** — the forked child survives and exits 1. It is `RET_ERRNO`, not fatal |

**What this changes.** The correct statement is **"no INET `bind`"**, not
"bindless". Two consequences, both of which a later session would otherwise get
wrong:

* ⭐ **A unix-socket relay works in this cage**, and dropssh already has it:
  `--relay unix://` (`transport.c` `transport_tcp_unix`, used by `serve.c:392`
  and by the e2e). This session's PoC ran a **real pubkey session to uid 0**
  through it. Any refusal of the unix-socket form justified by "the cage cannot
  bind" is wrong on this host, and one such refusal is corrected in the
  websocat issue.
* ⛔ **It is still a real wall for TCP.** Anything whose first step is a
  TCP listener in the cage is dead here. That part of every prior verdict
  stands.

**Why the wording matters:** dropssh's own `docs/relay-issues.md` and the
sandssh trackers say "cannot `bind(2)` even at uid 0", and the natural reading
of that is "no socket of any kind". The narrower claim is the one the
measurement supports.

## ⛔ Correction 2: the other 443-only egress claim, and what it does NOT cover

Re-measured today with an instrument that reads the proxy's **own status
line** over a raw socket (`experiments/40-confirm-egress-allowlist.sh`), on
**two identical rounds**, because one round is a coincidence not yet noticed:

```
example.com:443      200 Connection Established
github.com:443       200 Connection Established
cloudflare.com:443   200 Connection Established
1.1.1.1:443          200 Connection Established
bitbucket.org:443    200 Connection Established
example.com:22       403 not on the egress allowlist
github.com:22        403 not on the egress allowlist
example.com:8080     403 not on the egress allowlist
example.com:853      403 not on the egress allowlist
example.com:9999     403 not on the egress allowlist
```

**It is a PORT policy, not a host policy** — an allowlisted host on a non-443
port is refused with the same message, and a host not in any list (bitbucket)
is allowed on 443.

⛔ **What this does NOT establish, stated because it is easy to over-read:**
the earlier sweep in this project drew a conclusion about DoH on port 853 from
this table. **853 is refused, and dropssh's DoH is unaffected, because dropssh
resolves over HTTPS on 443** (`src/dns.c`, DoH over the same proxy the
transport uses). That is a `confirms` of solved work, not new work. ⛔ The
DNS experiments in the earlier sweep re-derive something `dropssh/src/dns.c`
already solves, and this session did not repeat them for that reason.

## The rest of the conditions, re-measured

| probe | result | why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/dev/ptmx` | **absent** | no pty. `script`, any PTY spawn, and any interactive-session test are dead here. Every session in this sweep is a **command** session. |
| `/etc/passwd` | **absent** | the condition dropssh's passwd shim exists for, and the one the FAKE_ROOT PoC reproduces. |
| `getpwnam('root')` | `KeyError` | as above. |
| UDP `bind` | **OK** | ⛔ do **not** assume "a cage has no UDP" as a general truth. It is true of the target cage per an earlier measurement; it is **not** true here, and UDP is not a dropssh dependency either way. |
| resolver (`getent hosts example.com`) | no answer | no working DNS. By-IP and DoH over the proxy are the paths, both already in `transport.c`/`dns.c`. |
| `strace`, `nc`, `patch(1)` | **absent** | three instruments had to be substituted; each first attempt failed and each failure is recorded below, because an instrument that reports a missing tool as a result is the exact defect this methodology exists to catch. |

## ⛔ What this did NOT establish

* **One machine, one day.** A cage with wider egress, or a real VPS, differs.
* **The target cage is not this sandbox.** This is a stand-in, and it is a
  *valid* one for the properties measured (no /etc/passwd, no /dev/ptmx, no
  resolver, 443-only egress, no INET bind) — but it is not the same kernel, and
  the INET-bind denial in particular is a property of *this* sandbox's seccomp
  profile.
* **No strace means no proof of the seccomp filter's exact shape.** The
  conclusion is drawn from the errno, the address-family split, and the
  surviving child, which is strong but is not a syscall trace.
* **Nothing was tested against the real ajam relay.** The multiplexed reverse
  path is untouched by this sweep.

## The three instruments that failed, and what replaced them

Recorded because each one first reported a **result** when it had actually
failed to run:

1. `40-` first used `curl` plus `nc`. `nc` is absent, so the raw `403` reply was
   never observed and the "not on the egress allowlist" text was **quoted from
   a previous session's notes**. Replaced with a raw socket, which reads the
   proxy's own status line.
2. The FAKE_ROOT PoC's apply step first used `patch(1)`. Absent. It reported
   "DOES NOT APPLY" for all nine files and **exited 0**. Replaced with
   `git apply --check`, and the script now exits 2 if neither is present.
3. The PoC's login observer first started `dropbear -i` on a shell redirect and
   reported `Failed socket address: Socket operation on non-socket` for both
   variants — that is the server refusing a **pipe**, not refusing to
   authenticate. Replaced by driving dropssh's own `serve` verb, which supplies
   the socketpair the inetd-pipe patch exists for.

## Re-run them

```sh
sh experiments/10-probe-the-cage.sh              # the conditions table
sh experiments/20-bind-tcp-vs-unix.sh            # the INET vs UNIX split
sh experiments/30-confirm-no-raw-sockets.sh      # control: bytes over AF_UNIX
sh experiments/40-confirm-egress-allowlist.sh    # 443-only, two rounds
```

title: Research: websocat and the Cloudflare any-TCP recipe — refuse, and it is a second confirmation of B4 and B7
body:
# Research: websocat and the Cloudflare any-TCP recipe — refuse, and it is a second confirmation of B4 and B7

Research unit, 2026-09-28. Method: TEMPLATE `docs/methodology/research.md`.
**Evidence. Nothing implemented.** A second read of a reference an earlier
sweep in this project already covered (sandssh #9, 2026-09-28), at the same
commit.

**Provenance (websocat).** `vi/websocat` at commit `3a3574cd2f5d`, mined
2026-09-28 (`mine-repo.sh`, route gh, control reachable, 0 gaps). Tracker:
309 issues+PRs both states, 1341 comments, 44 review comments, 0 discussions.
Three passes. Cite this commit beside every line.

**Provenance (the THC recipe).**
<https://iq.thc.org/tunnel-via-cloudflare-to-any-tcp-service>.
⛔ **Not read, and the reason is different from last time's "not archived":** a
web page is not a repository and this method mines repositories. Nothing below
depends on its contents; the verdict is derived from the measured host
constraint. Named as a gap so it is not mistaken for a source that was read.

## What websocat is, read from the tree

A byte-stream bridge: 11575 lines of Rust across 43 modules in `src/`. It is
"Netcat, curl and socat for WebSockets" (its README). A specifier names each
side (`exec:`, `sh-c:`, `cmd:`, `TcpListen`, `SOCKS5`, `unix:`, `file:`, …) and
it bridges them. **It is not a tunneler in the ngrok sense**: there is no
pairing, no rendezvous, no session identity.

The mechanism that matters to dropssh is `src/readdebt.rs`. `ReadDebt` exists
because a websocket is **message**-oriented and a byte stream is not: it
buffers a message that did not fit and offers three policies
(`DebtHandling::{Silent, Warn, DropMessage}`) plus `ZeroMessagesHandling`.
`README.md:528` states the consequence in one line: "Typically one line in
binary stream correspond to one WebSocket text message."

## ⛔ This is the second independent confirmation of dropssh's B4

`docs/relay-issues.md` B4: "`ws_read` is a byte stream, not a frame reader… It
is the root cause of B3 and of the class in `multiplexing.md`." A second
project, written in a different language, needed a whole module
(`readdebt.rs`) to hold the debt between "a message arrived" and "the buffer
had room", and had to make **what to do with a message that does not fit a
policy decision** (`Silent` / `Warn` / `DropMessage`).

⛔ **The adoptable half is that policy enum, not the module.** dropssh's B7
says "bounded queues with a documented overflow behaviour". `DropMessage` is
that behaviour, named, with a flag to choose it and a log line
(`error!("Dropping too large message...")`) that says which. dropssh's relay
currently has no policy for an oversized frame at all.

## The verdict on the Cloudflare any-TCP recipe, refused, with the measured reason

Read against what the cage can do, in the order the measurements decide it:

1. ⛔ **The "local listener" variant is dead, but the reason is not the one
   usually given.** The listener leg needs a TCP `bind`, and TCP `bind` fails
   at uid 0 here (`EACCES`, measured). The "client dials the worker" variant
   survives. Same wall every reference in this sweep hit.
   ⛔ **Correction to an earlier sweep in this project:** the general claim "the
   cage is bindless" is **too strong** and this session refuted it — AF_UNIX
   `bind`+`listen` **succeed** at uid 0 and carry real bytes between forked
   processes (`experiments/20-`, `30-`). The precise constraint is: **no INET
   `bind`**. Any verdict in this project resting on the broader wording should
   be narrowed.
2. ⚠ **Only 443 leaves the cage**, measured twice today with the proxy's own
   status line read back (`experiments/40-`): 443 → `200 Connection
   Established` for four hosts, and 22/8080/853/9999 → `403 not on the egress
   allowlist`. A Cloudflare worker is on 443, so this point is **survivable
   here**. Recorded because it would kill the recipe in most cages and here it
   does not.
3. ⛔ **dropssh already has a better first-party hop.** The ajam reverse relay
   is a multiplexer on 443 that a cage reaches today, proven live by the
   previous sweep's PoC. A worker is a **second** public service between cage
   and operator: a second failure domain, a second thing to page, and a
   capability (reach an arbitrary public TCP service) that is not the job.
   **The operator is already reachable. That is the job.**
4. ⚠ **A worker is a deploy, an account and a third party** the cage cannot
   provision. Cost measured in ongoing operational burden, not in lines.

## What to adopt

* ⛔ **Nothing from websocat itself.** dropssh's client is an ssh
  `ProxyCommand`; websocat is a debugging bridge. It is not a dependency: a
  Rust binary that must be present in a cage that takes one static C binary.
* ⚠ **Two ideas, both small, both inside work already queued:**
  * the **overflow policy enum** (`readdebt.rs:3-11`) belongs in B7's fix, as
    the named choices;
  * the **message-vs-byte discipline** is a `confirms` of B4 and of the
    `docs/multiplexing.md` row "`ws_read` returns 'whatever arrived', not one
    frame".
* ⚠ **A recipe, not a code path.** If a cage ever needs a public TCP service
  that is not ours, the shape is: dial the worker on 443 **through the CONNECT
  proxy** and splice stdio. Recorded so the next session starts from the
  measurement rather than from the THC page.

## What NOT to adopt

* ⛔ **A Cloudflare worker in the path.** Second hop, second operator, second
  thing to page.
* ⛔ **Reaching non-443 ports from the cage.** A hard wall here, measured.
* ⛔ **websocat as a dependency**, for the reason above.
* ⛔ Its own roadmap as a guide: `README.md:538` says v1 "is based on obsolete
  dependency versions that trigger security warnings" and v4 "is not yet
  considered stable and has many missing features". Not our problem, but it is
  a reason not to build on either line.

## Tracker findings the code does not say

* ⛔ **`README.md:535`, in its own words**: "Current version of Websocat don't
  receive notification about closed sockets. This makes serving without `-E`
  or `-u` options or in backpressure scenarios **prone to socket leak**." And
  two open issues say the same: **#35** "Websocat in servermode eating a CPU
  core after closing TCP socket" and **#13** "Socket leak unless -E".
  **This is dropssh's B7 class (no backpressure/teardown) from a fourth
  independent project** in this project's sweep, after chisel, sshx and
  ligolo-ng. Four projects reporting the same class is the strongest signal in
  the corpus, and it says *lifecycle and teardown, not forwarding* is what
  these tools break on.
* ⛔ **#99 "SSH through CDN"** and **#102 "corporate proxy with auth"** (both
  closed): users doing dropssh's job with websocat. **The need is real and the
  tool is not the answer** — the need is B1 through B5.
* ⛔ **#255 (open) Unix Domain Socket**: the "relay over a bindless cage on a
  unix socket" shape. ⛔ `confirms`, and now with a measurement behind it: the
  unix-socket relay is not a workaround, it is the only relay form that works
  in this cage (`experiments/20-`, and dropssh's own `--relay unix://`).
  **#37 (PROXY protocol) and #262 (ALPN)** are also open upstream; the proxy
  one is the shape dropssh already implements in `transport.c`.

## ⛔ What was NOT established

* **The Cloudflare recipe was not read and not tested**, and no worker was
  deployed. Whether a Cloudflare worker can open a TCP socket to an arbitrary
  host is a question about Cloudflare's platform that was **not** answered
  here. The verdict does not depend on it: the recipe is refused because
  dropssh has a better first-party hop and the cage cannot deploy a worker, not
  because a worker cannot splice.
* **websocat was not built or run.** The verdict is read from `README.md`,
  `src/readdebt.rs` and the tracker.
* **Zero discussions were fetched** (the route cannot reach them
  credential-free), so websocat's own design argument is unread.
* The "4th project" count is a count within this project's sweeps, not a
  claim about the wider ecosystem.
* One machine, one day.

title: Research: wiretap — refuse the architecture, and the one capability it points at is dropssh's to add
body:
# Research: wiretap — refuse the architecture, and the one capability it points at is dropssh's to add

Research unit, 2026-09-28. Method: TEMPLATE `docs/methodology/research.md`.
**Evidence. Nothing implemented.** A second read of a reference an earlier
sweep in this project already covered (sandssh #6, 2026-09-28), at the same
commit. What follows is the re-read, and **what changed**.

**Provenance.** `sandialabs/wiretap` at commit `104be99c29e8`, mined
2026-09-28 (`mine-repo.sh`, route gh, control reachable, 0 gaps). Tracker:
109 issues+PRs **both states**, 155 comments, 114 review comments, 3
discussions. Three passes, plus the claim audit. Cite this commit beside
every line.

## What it is, and the sentence that decides the verdict

A WireGuard mesh with a gVisor userspace stack. `README.md:56`:
"**Privileged access necessary to configure WireGuard interfaces**";
`README.md:66`: "**Bidirectional UDP communication between Server and Client
on one port**". `README.md:98` explains the userspace stack exists to "reroute
traffic to a user-space TCP/IP network stack, where a listener accepts
connections **on behalf of the true destination**".

**⛔ The question names `wiretap#tcp-tunneling`, and that section does not
change the verdict — here is why, precisely.** `README.md:572-585` is
WireGuard-over-TCP (udptunnel / `chisel` / `socat` as the workarounds it names),
not a TCP transport that dropssh could use. Its own warning is "Performance
will suffer, only use TCP Tunneling as a last resort". The **dependency** of
that path is still the WireGuard interface, which is the thing the cage cannot
provide. So the named section is refused for a reason that is in the section
itself, not inferred from the README's summary.

## What to adopt

1. ⭐ **The capability, not the code: a server-side SOCKS5 that reaches a
   client.** `expose --dynamic` (`src/cmd/expose.go:54`) opens a SOCKS5
   **on the remote port**, and `src/transport/transport.go:445-476`
   (`ForwardDynamic`) is the implementation: it builds a `socks5.Config` whose
   `Dial` closure dials through the userspace stack, and serves it on a
   listener. `README.md:483-492` documents the use:
   `curl -x socks5://<server-ip>:8080 http://<any-ip>:80`.

   ⛔ **Two properties worth taking, one of them a decision to make on
   purpose.** The listener is on the **operator**, which is the only place it
   can be — that part is a `confirms` of dropssh's posture, not new work. And
   `README.md:481`: "If a Wiretap Server process exits or dies for any reason
   it will not remember ports it was previously exposing." **A relay that
   forgets its forwards on restart** is a property to choose deliberately, and
   dropssh's relay (`src/relay.c`) currently has no equivalent state at all.

   ⛔ **Cost note that corrects an earlier claim in this project.** The
   earlier sweep filed this as "a dropssh gap" and called it missing. The gap
   is real — `grep -rni socks src/ tests/ docs/` in dropssh finds only the
   token `sockstate` in `transport.c` and nothing that speaks SOCKS5 — but it
   is **not blocked by the cage**: the listener belongs on the operator, and
   an operator machine can bind. What it costs in dropssh is a
   `socks5_config` parse and a `CONNECT` in `connect.c` or a new verb, not a
   capability that only a router-shaped tool can provide.

2. **E2EE nested inside a relay that cannot read it.**
   `src/transport/userspace/bind.go` (`UserspaceSocketBind`, adapted from
   wireguard-go) is the shape. ⛔ `confirms` what dropssh already has, with
   better reasoning: dropssh's E2EE is ssh's, so dropbear is already the
   server and a relay compromise yields ciphertext. The README's own statement
   (`:100`) — the relay interface "cannot see the plaintext" — is the property
   already in dropssh's `AGENTS.md`.

## What NOT to adopt

* ⛔ **WireGuard as the transport.** TUN, privileged routing, bidirectional UDP
  — and the cage's egress answers `403 not on the egress allowlist` on every
  non-443 port, measured twice today with the proxy's own status line
  (`experiments/40-`). Independently, wiretap's own **#61** ("WG is not
  actual") reports WireGuard blocked in some jurisdictions.
* ⛔ **gVisor `netstack`.** `src/transport/tcp/tcp.go` is vendored tailscale
  netstack (`:4-5` credits the upstream) and its dependency is *the interface*,
  not the forwarding. A userspace IP stack exists to present a routed IP
  interface; ssh gives a byte stream and a login.
* ⛔ **The REST control plane.** `src/api/api.go:185` `Expose(..., dynamic bool)`
  POSTs to an API port, and **#20** proposed it. A new surface. dropssh's
  honest version of "tell me what is happening" is structured events on stderr
  (R4), not an API.
* ⛔ **The two-interface Relay/E2EE model.** #11 is the cost evidence, from
  users: two interfaces for a one-hop tunnel is a burden its own users asked
  to remove (`--simple` was the fix). dropssh's model is one relay, one
  binary, one session.

## Tracker findings the code does not say

* ⛔ **#16 (closed)**: ~14 MB rss per TCP connection, OOM-killed at ~88k conns on
  2 GB. ⛔ The reporter's figure is from an nmap/masscan load on v0.2.0, 2023
  vintage, not a controlled benchmark. It is a **cost signal about gVisor
  stacks**, and the most useful number in this tracker.
* ⛔ **#15 (closed)**: userspace SYN-SENT exhaustion under scans; the fix was a
  `--conn-timeout` that kills the exit-node→target wait. The maintainer's own
  comment: the timeout "**just** kills the exit node -> target connection so it
  stops waiting for a SYNACK. No RST is sent back to the origin server." A
  precise statement of a lifecycle rule dropssh's B7 needs.
* ⛔ **#22 (closed)**: users asked for a PTY shell on the exit node for
  *recovery* access, and the maintainer declined. ⛔ **Dead on arrival here
  anyway**: this cage has no `/dev/ptmx` (measured, `experiments/10-`).
  Recorded so it is not re-proposed.
* **#81 (open) Regression Testing**, **#64 (open) Transport Plugins**,
  **#60 (open) Attach error nodes to network tree**: an active project with
  open work. Not a reason either way for dropssh; recorded so the reference is
  not mistaken for abandoned.

## ⛔ What changed on the re-read, and what did not

* ⛔ **What did NOT change:** the architecture refusal, the two-interface model
  refusal, the gVisor refusal. All re-read against source at the same commit
  and all hold. The 14 MB/connection figure in #16 was re-read and is
  **downgraded to an explicitly-labelled estimate** rather than a cost of the
  design.
* ⚠ **What DID change:** the SOCKS capability is no longer filed as a gap with
  an unknown owner. It is now scoped: a `CONNECT` handler on the operator side
  of `dropssh relay`, plus the decision about whether forwards survive a
  restart. That is a different, actionable statement than "dropssh has no
  SOCKS".

## ⛔ What was NOT established

* **wiretap was not run.** Not built, not started, no session. The verdict is
  structural, read from `README.md` and `src/`.
* **The gVisor memory figure is a reporter's load test**, not a measurement of
  anything on this machine or on dropssh.
* **SOCKS5 was not implemented and not tested** in dropssh. The scope above is
  what it would take, not a proof it would work.
* **3 discussions were fetched**; the design argument in them was not read in
  full, so the maintainer's reasoning about the netstack is taken from code
  and README rather than from the discussion where it may be argued.
* One machine, one day.

title: Research: dropbear-sshj — refuse it, and record the one thing it proves about R9
body:
# Research: dropbear-sshj — refuse it, and record the one thing it proves about R9

Research unit, 2026-09-28. Method: TEMPLATE `docs/methodology/research.md`.
**Evidence. Nothing implemented.**

**Provenance.** `ValdikSS/dropbear-sshj` at commit `d622b1e8fe35`, cloned
2026-09-28 from `https://bitbucket.org/ValdikSS/dropbear-sshj.git`.
⛔ **Route differs from the other three references and the reason is stated:**
Bitbucket does not serve the GitHub API, and its 2.0 issues endpoint now
answers `{"error": {"message": "CHANGE-3071 - Functionality has been
deprecated"}}`. **Its tracker is unreachable from here.** That is a measured
gap, not an unattempted step. Cite this commit beside every line.

## What it is, and how little of it there is

A full dropbear fork (2020.81) with vendored libtomcrypt/libtommath, and
**exactly one commit by one author on top of upstream**:

```
1462  Matt Johnston <matt@ucc.asn.au>      <- upstream dropbear
  33  Gaël PORTAY                            <- debian packaging
  1   ValdikSS <iam@valdikss.org.ru>         <- d622b1e "SSH-J.com improvements"
```

That single commit is 475 insertions across 14 files, and its own README says
what it is worth:

> "The code is bad and provided as-is. After I made the PoC modifications…
> I found functionally better and mature project called sish… **Please use
> sish, don't use my hack.** The code is provided for research and archiving
> purposes only… The code is non-portable."

**A tracker the method reached for and could not.** The project names
https://github.com/antoniomika/sish as the thing that supersedes it. That is
the maintainer saying, in the project's own words, "this is archaeology". It is
not a reason to refuse it on its own — anti-pattern exhibits are kept **on
purpose** — so it was read anyway.

## Why it is refused, with the reason that decides it

**It changes the exact function R9 is about, in the unsafe direction.**
`common-session.c:148`, in the one commit:

```diff
-	ses.allowprivport = 0;
+	ses.allowprivport = 1;
```

`allowprivport` is dropbear's switch for binding privileged ports in
`direct-tcpip` forwarding. The entire purpose of this fork is to publish
arbitrary ports, so it turns that on globally. dropssh's cage is a single-user
box whose ssh server is reached through a socketpair and never forwards a port
at all. Adopting any of this fork's `common-session.c` changes R9's
implementation from a review of three lines into a review of a security
posture change, and that is the wrong trade for the goal.

**The pseudodns is a rendezvous service dropssh already has, worse.**
`srv-tcpfwd-pseudodns.c` (306 lines) forks a second process at startup
(`svr-main.c:165-167`), binds an abstract unix socket
(`PSEUDODNS_SOCK_NAME "@/dropbear/pseudodns"`, `default_options.h:330`), and
holds a 20-entry table of `username -> (requested host, requested port) ->
real port` so that a user can publish `ssh anyuser@ssh-j.com -R
laptop-behind-nat:22:localhost:22` and be reached at a **DNS name instead of a
port number** (`svr-tcpfwd.c:204-244` rewrites the destination host to
`localhost` and the port to the allocated one). That is a naming layer over
port forwarding.

⛔ **Its `pseudodns_get_entry` is also a socket round-trip per lookup**, and on
any error it returns **0**, which the caller then reads as "no such mapping,
refuse the connection" `svr-tcpfwd.c:315-319`, with the comment
`// 0 is here for a reason, not a mistake` at line 274). A transient error and
a genuine miss are the same value. dropssh relays session bytes; a failure that
looks like a miss is the class of bug in `docs/relay-issues.md` B11/B12.

**⛔ The one place I am least sure, stated rather than hidden.** The natural
refusal reason is "a public SOCKS needs a listener, and the cage cannot bind".
This session **refuted that reason**: AF_UNIX `bind`+`listen` succeed at uid 0
here (`experiments/20-`, `30-`), and dropssh's own `--relay unix://` works. So
the refusal rests on the **deployment shape** instead — a shared server
exposing one SOCKS-ish port for many usernames, a 20-entry global table with a
per-user cap of 4 (`default_options.h:327-329`), and a mapping that any
user reaching the port could use. That is a multi-tenant public service, which
is not what dropssh is, and **it was not run**.

## What to adopt

* ⛔ **Nothing as code.** The `IMPERSONATE_ALL_USERS` machinery
  (`svr-auth.c:98-100`, `auth.h:97-99`) is the one idea with a shape worth
  knowing: it keeps the client-presented name in `orig_username` while
  authenticating and running as a fixed account. It is **not wanted** here
  (dropssh is uid 0 in a one-user cage by design) and it is dangerous: with
  `IMPERSONATE_FORCE_PASSWORDLESS_AUTH` it calls `send_msg_userauth_success()`
  before any credential check (`svr-authpasswd.c:83-86`). Recorded so nobody
  proposes it as a "no passwd" fix.
* ⭐ **One thing it proves about R9, which is worth having.** Its
  `MAX_HOST_LEN 254 -> 64` change (`sysoptions.h:63`) shows that a fork
  touching `svr-tcpfwd.c` **also** has to touch the address-length check in
  `svr_cancelremotetcp` and `svr_remotetcpreq` (both at lines 147 and 182).
  dropssh's R9 does not touch forwarding at all, so this cost does not apply
  to R9 — but it is the reason a second author's patch to the same file should
  be read as a whole rather than as hunks.

## What NOT to adopt

* ⛔ **The fork, or any part of it.** One author's one commit, self-described as
  bad and superseded, a decade behind, on a different version, against a
  different goal.
* ⛔ `allowprivport = 1`.
* ⛔ The pseudodns: a fixed 20-entry table, a per-user cap, a forked process
  and a unix-socket RPC per lookup, error-as-miss, and a public multi-tenant
  shape.
* ⛔ `MAX_HOST_LEN 254 -> 64`: it would **shorten** what dropssh's forwarding
  accepts. The direction is wrong here.
* ⛔ It is not a tracker-less project — its tracker is simply **unreachable**
  from this method. Recorded as a gap in the provenance, not as a clean sweep.

## ⛔ What was NOT established

* **The tracker was never read.** Bitbucket's issues API is deprecated (the
  exact error is above) and no substitute was used. If that project has
  recorded failures, they are not in this sweep.
* **It was not built or run.** No compile, no session. The verdict is
  structural, read from the diff and the README.
* **sish was not read**, even though the fork names it as the successor. A
  session that wants a public-jump-host reference should read sish, not this.
* One commit by one author, so "how does this project behave over time" has no
  answer here.

title: Research: dropbear-hacks FAKE_ROOT — R9's route is real, measured on the pinned dropbear
body:
# Research: dropbear-hacks FAKE_ROOT — R9's route is real, measured on the pinned dropbear

Research unit, 2026-09-28. Method: TEMPLATE `docs/methodology/research.md`.
**Evidence and a proof of concept. Nothing is implemented; no tree is touched.**

**Provenance.** `zcutlip/dropbear-hacks` at commit `5bb72e13b7ee`, mined
2026-09-28 with `scripts/common/mine-repo.sh` (route gh, control reachable,
0 gaps). Tracker: **0 issues, 0 comments, 0 review comments, 0 discussions**.
The tree is a README, a Makefile, `buildmips.sh` and two patches
(`hacks_to_dropbear-2013.58.patch`, `hacks_to_dropbear-2016.74.patch`). Both
patches carry the same mechanism; the 2016.74 one is the one read. Four
passes. Cite this commit beside every line.

## What it is

A dropbear fork for embedded systems with no passwd database. Its README says
the problem exactly: "many embedded systems lack any sort of mapping between
usernames, including 'root'… attempting to log into an SSH server as root
results in a failure due to an uninitialized passwd struct from getpwnam()".
That is dropssh's cage, stated in 2017.

Three mechanisms, not one:

| mechanism | where | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FAKE_ROOT` | `hacks_to_dropbear-2016.74.patch` lines 24-65 (`get_fake_pwnam` + the `fill_passwd` fallback), plus call sites in `loginrec.c:140-146` and `svr-chansession.c:250-256` | when `getpwnam` returns NULL **and** the name is `root`, return a synthetic `struct passwd` with uid/gid 0, dir `/`, shell `/bin/sh` |
| `ALT_SHELL` | lines 9-14 (`get_user_shell`) and `compat.c:99-103` (`initshells`) | a compile-time alternate shell, **and** it is added to dropbear's `okshells` list so the login-shell check accepts it |
| master password `-Y`, forced home `-H` | `svr-auth.c:204-213`, `svr-runopts.c:268/277/304/314/327-341` | overwrite `pw_passwd` and `pw_dir` for every session |

## ⛔ What is already ours, and is the most important line here

**dropssh already ships the file-driven form of this, out of process.**
`fakepwd.so` interposes `getpwnam` and `getpwnam_r` and reads a passwd file
from `$SANDHOME_PASSWD` (observed with `strings` on the built artefact, and
`serve.c:299-304` sets that variable for the server child). So the
**capability** is `confirms`, not `adopt`.

What FAKE_ROOT adds is the **location**: it moves the fallback *inside* the
server, which is what R9 asks for. That is a real difference and it is worth
exactly one thing: it removes the `LD_PRELOAD` dependency, and with it the
glibc/musl split documented in `AGENTS.md` ("a musl dropbear cannot be
interposed at all"), so a **static** server becomes usable.

## What was measured, on the pinned dropbear, through a real session

dropssh was built here (`scripts/build.sh --target x86_64-linux-musl`, exit 0)
and its gate is green (`tests/e2e.sh`, 9 passed, 0 failed). The pinned dropbear
is `59870ad43153`, version **2026.94**, at the commit dropssh fetches.

1. **The 2016.74 patch is 10 years behind the pinned dropbear and mostly still
   applies**: `git apply --check` per file gives **4 of 9 clean** —
   `common-session.c`, `loginrec.c`, `session.h`, `svr-chansession.c` — and
   **all three of FAKE_ROOT's own files are among the four that apply**. The
   five that fail (`compat.c`, `options.h`, `runopts.h`, `svr-auth.c`,
   `svr-runopts.c`) are all `ALT_SHELL` or the `-Y`/`-H` half, not FAKE_ROOT.
2. **It compiles.** Transcribing only the mechanism (not the patch) into the
   pinned source and relinking gives a working `dropbear` (2550920 bytes).
3. **It changes the observable outcome.** Two runs, same command, the only
   variable being which dropbear binary is behind the socketpair, driven
   through dropssh's own `serve` and `connect` verbs with a real `ssh` client,
   `LD_PRELOAD` unset in the server's environment in both:

```
--- unpatched dropbear (dropssh's own build) ---
  server stdout: (empty)
  [49980] Login attempt for nonexistent user from localhost:...
  [49980] Exit before auth from <localhost:...>: Exited normally

--- FAKE_ROOT dropbear ---
  server stdout: 0
  [50029] Pubkey auth succeeded for 'root' with ssh-ed25519 key SHA256:...
  [50029] initgroups: Operation not permitted (continuing: gid unchanged)
```

Reproduced twice, identical, **exit 0 both times**, read unpiped.

**The whole point of the mechanism is the difference between those two log
lines**, and both are already in dropssh's error vocabulary. `Exit before auth`
is named in `docs/multiplexing.md` as the message that has meant three
different things; here it means *the passwd lookup*, and the fix is legible
from the log alone.

## What to adopt

1. **The in-tree passwd fallback for R9.** Not this patch: the mechanism. R9
   says "a `--passwd-file` option patched into dropbear"; that is the right
   shape and FAKE_ROOT is proof it can be done on the pinned commit.
2. **The door-sweep result, which is the part that makes it three lines and not
   five.** Every `getpwnam`/`getpwuid` in the pinned dropbear is
   `common-session.c:667`, `loginrec.c:270`, `svr-chansession.c:625` (the three
   FAKE_ROOT patches) and `cli-kex.c:276`, `cli-runopts.c:836`,
   `dbutil.c:715`, `dropbearkey.c:411`. **The other four are `getpwuid(getuid())`
   and every one of them already degrades**: null-checked `pw`, `HOME` read
   from the environment first, or a logged warning
   (`cli-runopts.c:840-841` "failed to identify current user. Trying
   anyway."). So the patch author's three call sites are exactly the ones that
   hard-fail. A patch that covered all seven would be four lines longer and
   fix nothing.
3. **`ALT_SHELL`'s `initshells` half as prior art, not as a change.** dropssh's
   `patches/dropbear-login-shell-tolerance.patch` already solves the login-shell
   problem better (it consults the list first and then accepts an executable
   shell, so a host with a policy keeps it). Recorded so nobody re-derives it.

## What NOT to adopt

* ⛔ **The code.** It is a patch against 2016.74, five of nine files do not
  apply, and dropssh's convention is that no dropbear code is copied
  (`AGENTS.md`: "three diffs against dropbear; no dropbear code is copied").
  Transcribe the mechanism, write dropssh's own diff.
* ⛔ **`-Y` master password.** It **logs the password in plaintext on startup,
  twice** (`svr-runopts.c:330-338`: `"Plaintext: %s"` and `"crypted: %s"`), and
  it overwrites `pw_passwd` for **every** session
  (`svr-auth.c:204-210`), which silently disables the real account's password
  check. A footgun that also leaks. Refused.
* ⛔ **The hard-coded root as the shipped behaviour.** FAKE_ROOT invents uid 0
  for anyone who asks for `root`. Fine for a one-user cage, wrong the moment
  the server is reachable by more than one name. dropssh's `--passwd FILE`
  already has the right shape: the file says who exists.
* ⛔ `-H` forced home: `pw_dir = "/"` is already the FAKE_ROOT default and a
  forced home has no caller in dropssh.

## ⛔ What was NOT established

* **One dropbear commit.** Only `59870ad43153` / 2026.94 was tested. The patch
  is written for 2016.74 and 4/9 hunks applying says nothing about any other
  commit.
* **Not a finished R9 patch.** The PoC transcribes the mechanism to answer one
  question. It has no `--passwd-file` option, no file parsing, no tests, and it
  is not a drop-in. That is the implementing session's work.
* **No interactive session.** This cage has no `/dev/ptmx`, so every session
  here is a command session. `pty_setowner` (`svr-chansession.c`) is on the
  patched path and is therefore **untested**.
* **No multi-user host.** FAKE_ROOT's safety argument is untested and the
  "-Y" objection above is the one that matters.
* **`fakepwd.so` was not disassembled**; its behaviour was read from
  `strings` on the built artefact and from `serve.c:299-304`.

## Re-run it

```sh
sh poc/10-dropbear-hacks-fake-root.sh        # exit 0 = confirmed
```
Conditions are printed by the script. Machine: Linux 6.18.54, uid 0,
2026-09-28, zig 0.13.0, dropbear 2026.94 at the pinned commit.

**⛔ A note on the instrument, because it failed first.** `patch(1)` is
**absent** in this cage, so the first run reported "DOES NOT APPLY" for all
nine files and **exited 0** — a missing tool reported as a result. The
substitute is `git apply --check`, and the script now refuses to run without
one. A second failure: the mutation that stopped the mechanism being inserted
still reported `CONFIRMED`, because a stale build directory made "the
FAKE_ROOT dropbear" an old binary. The PoC now cleans its tree and asserts
`fallback call sites inserted >= 2` before it will report anything; that guard
was re-run against the planted defect (**exit 1**) and against the correct
input (**exit 0**).
